target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would remove unequal access barriers to voting
objection: AG2 argues that federal holiday status does not require private employers to give paid time off or close, so many low-income workers—especially in retail, food service, and other hourly jobs—would still have to choose between wages and voting.

target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday by itself is an effective turnout strategy
objection: AG2 says research does not show that making Election Day a holiday alone reliably increases turnout compared with broader access reforms like employer time-off rules and automatic voter registration.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday leaves the scheduling barrier intact for low-income workers
objection: AG1 responds that the holiday should not be treated as a standalone policy and that it still changes the baseline schedule by shifting schools, workplaces, transit, and childcare routines, thereby reducing day-of conflicts for many voters.

target: AG1’s response that a holiday meaningfully reduces scheduling friction even without guaranteed paid leave
objection: AG2 objects that private retail and service employers can remain open, so without enforceable paid time-to-vote rules the holiday does not reliably create a right to time off and may be redundant or insufficient.

target: AG2’s view that the holiday is redundant because time-to-vote rules are the real solution
objection: AG1 argues that a national holiday still changes the default environment nationwide and complements time-to-vote rules by making Election Day a system-wide event rather than a patchwork of workplace negotiations.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday reduces scheduling barriers at scale
objection: AG2 says holiday status does not ensure paid time off or enforceable time-to-vote rights, and that private employers and essential services can largely ignore the federal holiday, leaving low-income workers exposed to the same barriers.

target: AG2’s contention that only enforceable workplace rules matter
objection: AG1 argues that the holiday makes time-to-vote rules easier to implement and comply with by creating a common non-workday baseline, so the holiday is a practical complement rather than a substitute.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday makes time-to-vote rules easier to implement
objection: AG2 says the holiday still does not secure paid or guaranteed time for hourly low-wage workers in sectors that stay open, so the key right remains unprotected unless separately mandated.

target: AG2’s argument that open essential jobs defeat the value of a holiday
objection: AG1 says the holiday still reduces default scheduling conflicts, lowers school/childcare friction, and makes voting easier for many people even when some workers need additional protections.

target: AG1’s view that a holiday broadly lowers practical friction
objection: AG2 replies that low-income workers in open, customer-facing, or essential jobs still face the wage-time tradeoff and may also encounter reduced transit or service availability on a holiday, creating new barriers.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday does not meaningfully change access for hourly workers
objection: AG1 argues that federal holidays often change employer scheduling and staffing behavior in practice, so many workers benefit even without a specific paid-leave mandate.

target: AG1’s assertion that a federal holiday would materially help hourly workers
objection: AG2 concedes some workplaces would help, but says the policy is uneven and can become a substitute that diverts attention from stronger, enforceable reforms such as paid time-to-vote, staffing, and registration fixes.

target: AG2’s concern that the holiday is a blunt, possibly substitutive policy
objection: AG1 adds that a holiday reduces childcare and logistical burdens for parents by making Election Day a non-school day, lowering the overall time-and-logistics burden on families with limited flexibility.

target: AG1’s childcare/logistics argument
objection: AG2 says school closure does not ensure affordable or available childcare and may simply shift the burden, while the core problem for many workers remains lost wages and lack of guaranteed paid time to vote.

target: AG2’s claim that the childcare benefit is too narrow and indirect
objection: AG1 responds that the holiday need not solve every barrier and that a day-off from school still reduces day-of friction for many families, even if some childcare costs remain.

target: AG1’s focus on day-of scheduling relief
objection: AG2 argues that a national Election Day holiday does not fix pre-election administrative barriers such as registration or eligibility problems, so it is poorly targeted compared with direct access reforms.

target: AG2’s claim that administrative barriers make the holiday inadequate
objection: AG1 says the holiday addresses the widest, most universal bottleneck—the need to fit voting into a normal weekday—while complementing, not preventing, administrative reforms.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday is a broad barrier-reducer
objection: AG2 says the holiday is still an unreliable and potentially regressive lever because some low-wage workers could be forced into unpaid holiday time off, reduced hours, or unscheduled shift changes instead of protected paid time to vote.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday scheduling can hurt low-income workers
objection: AG1 argues that a national holiday can also increase election capacity by making it easier to recruit poll workers and volunteers, which can reduce lines and last-mile voting friction.

target: AG1’s capacity argument
objection: AG2 replies that polling places are not staffed mainly by free volunteers and that a calendar holiday does not guarantee enough additional staff, machines, or sites to solve capacity problems, especially for low-income communities.

target: AG2’s claim that workers still face the same barriers despite a holiday
objection: AG1 says enforceable time-to-vote rules require transaction costs and active enforcement, while a holiday changes the default calendar and reduces the need for workers to ask, negotiate, or report violations in the first place.

target: AG1’s claim that a shared civic day reduces workers’ transaction costs
objection: AG2 says the holiday still does not guarantee paid, protected time and therefore can leave the core wage-loss and shift-disruption tradeoff intact for hourly low-wage workers.
